items.name: Sarazm: Central Asia's first farming town
items.description: Sarazm, on the left bank of the Zarafshan about 15 km west of Panjakent, is one of the oldest settled sites in Central Asia, with radiocarbon dates from about 3900 to 2100 BCE. At its height it covered up to 90 hectares. It was the most north-easterly of the proto-historic farming settlements of the region, and it traded with a network of settlements reaching from the Turkmen steppes and the Aral Sea to the Iranian plateau and the Indus. Found after farmers turned up objects in their fields, it was first excavated in 1977 by Abdullah Isakov of the Tajik Academy of Sciences, later with French (CNRS) teams. In 2010 it became Tajikistan's first World Heritage Site.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage — Proto-urban Site of Sarazm

items.name: Bactria, Sogdiana and Alexander's 'Furthest Alexandria'
items.description: Under the Achaemenid Persians, Sogdiana (the Zarafshan and Kashkadarya valleys) and Bactria (between the Hindu Kush and the Amu Darya, with part of today's south Tajikistan) were satrapies of the empire. Cyrus the Great founded Cyropolis to mark its north-eastern border; its site is unknown, and Khujand, Istaravshan and Kurkath have all been proposed. In 329 BCE Alexander the Great took Cyropolis and six other towns, and in August founded Alexandria Eschate, 'the Furthest Alexandria', on the Syr Darya at or near Khujand. The Sogdian Spitamenes led a revolt that cost Alexander a whole column; in spring 327 BCE Alexander's climbers took the 'impregnable' Sogdian Rock, where Oxyartes had sent his family, and Alexander married his daughter Roxana.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Siege of the Sogdian Rock

items.name: Takht-i Sangin and the Greco-Bactrian Oxus
items.description: After Alexander, the Seleucids and then the Greco-Bactrian kings held Bactria and Sogdiana for about two hundred years. At Takht-i Sangin, where the Vakhsh and the Panj meet to form the Amu Darya (the ancient Oxus), a Temple of the Oxus was built around 300 BCE, perhaps with Seleucid money, inside a walled town; it may have been the central shrine of the river god for the whole of Bactria, and the site may be the source of the Oxus Treasure. Near Kulob a Greek inscription of 200–195 BCE records a man named Heliodotos dedicating a fire altar to Hestia for King Euthydemus I and his son Demetrius. The town was sacked in the 130s BCE, probably by the nomads who became the Kushans, but the temple stayed in use into the 3rd century CE.

items.name: The Yuezhi and the Kushan Empire
items.description: From about 90 to 30 BCE the Yuezhi, nomads from the east, destroyed the last Hellenistic states in Bactria and, with the related Tokhari, founded the Kushan Empire around 30 CE. For the next four centuries the Kushans were one of the great powers of their age, alongside Rome, Parthia and Han China, and Bactria, which later took the name Tokharistan, was its heartland north of the Hindu Kush. The Kushan king Kanishka promoted Buddhism, and in this period Buddhism spread from Central Asia to China. At the end of the period the shrunken Kushan realm had to defend itself against the Sasanian Persians, who held much of today's Tajikistan before the Hephthalites took it.

items.name: The Hephthalites, the 'White Huns' of Tokharistan
items.description: The Hephthalites became a power in Bactria around 450 CE, displacing the Kidarites (in Tokharistan probably by 466). Their stronghold was Tokharistan, and their capital was probably Kunduz; they wrote Bactrian in Greek letters and called themselves Ebodalo. By 479 (or 509) they had conquered Sogdia, and Ustrushana was part of their realm. The Sasanian king Peroz I, whom they had helped to the throne, fought three wars with them: he was twice captured and ransomed, and in 484 he was killed near Herat by the Hephthalite king, after which Persia paid them tribute. Around 557 the Göktürks and the Sasanians under Khosrow I defeated them in an eight-day battle near Qarshi, and the empire broke up into principalities under Turkic or Persian overlords, among them Chaghaniyan and Khuttal in today's south Tajikistan.

items.name: The Yabghus of Tokharistan and the Buddhist monasteries
items.description: In 625 the Western Turkic qaghan Tong Yabghu invaded Tokharistan, made the Hephthalite principalities submit and installed his son Tardush Shad as yabghu (sub-king) of Tokharistan at Kunduz. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited Tardush there in 630, shortly before his son poisoned him. A Chinese list names the yabghus' vassal kingdoms, among them Khuttal, Chaghaniyan, Shughnan, Wakhan, Kobadiyan and Badakhshan, all in or beside today's Tajikistan. Buddhism revived under the Western Turks: monasteries of the 7th–8th centuries such as Ajina Tepe near Bokhtar and Qal'a-i Kafirnihan have yielded Buddhist art. The Arabs took Balkh in 652–653; Qutayba ibn Muslim made Chaghaniyan submit in 705 and in 710 sent the yabghu to Damascus as a hostage, but the dynasty survived in Badakhshan until at least 758, and Khuttal held out until the Abbasids took it over in 750–751.

items.name: Ustrushana and the afshins
items.description: Ustrushana lay south of the great bend of the Syr Darya, roughly between Samarkand and Khujand, with its capital at Bunjikat (near today's Shahristan). Closely tied to Sogdia, it was ruled by princes with the title afshin, under the Hephthalites and from about 560 under the Western Turks. Qutayba ibn Muslim's invasion of 712–714 did not bring it under Arab control; Nasr ibn Sayyar subdued it only partly in 739, and only in 794–795 did the afshin Karakana submit to the Barmakid al-Fadl ibn Yahya. After the afshin Kawus broke away again, an Abbasid army guided by his son Khaydhar conquered it for good in 822. Khaydhar, known as al-Afshin, became a great general of the caliph al-Mu'tasim and fought the Khurramite rebel Babak Khorramdin, but in 841 he was arrested in Samarra on suspicion of plotting against the Abbasids and died in captivity. His dynasty ruled Ustrushana until 893, when it became a Samanid province.

items.name: Panjikent, Devashtich and Mount Mugh
items.description: Panjikent, on the Zarafshan, was a small but flourishing Sogdian town that grew from the 5th century; its murals, now in the Hermitage and in the National Museum of Antiquities in Dushanbe, mix Greek styles, the Iranian epic of Rostam and local, Iranian and Hindu gods. Around 706 the Sogdian noble Devashtich was elected its king; he called himself 'Sogdian king' and 'ruler of Samarkand', and accepted Umayyad authority after Qutayba's invasion of 712. In 720 he joined a Sogdian revolt against the Arabs. Defeated near Panjikent in 722, he fled to a mountain fortress on Mount Mugh, 60 km up the Zarafshan, surrendered, and was executed that autumn. Panjikent was ruled by Arab administrators for about fifty years, and by the end of the 8th century the old town was abandoned.

items.name: The Samanids and Rudaki, 'father of Tajik literature'
items.description: The Samanids, descended from Saman Khuda, were one of the first native Persian dynasties after the Arab conquest. From 819 they governed Transoxiana for the Abbasid caliphs, and under Isma'il Samani (892–907), who beat the Saffarids in 900, they ruled Khurasan as well from their capital, Bukhara. Bukhara and Samarkand became centres of art, science and literature, and New Persian literature flourished. Rudaki (c. 858–941), born near Samarkand (Sadriddin Ayni identified his birthplace as Panjrud in the Panjakent district), was a court poet of the Samanids and is honoured in Tajikistan as the 'father of Tajik literature'. Khuttal, ruled by a branch of the Banijurids, acknowledged Samanid overlordship in the 10th century. Weakened after 950, the Samanids lost their lands south of the Oxus to the Ghaznavids, and in 999 the Karakhanids took Bukhara.

items.name: Khuttal, the Turkic dynasties and Nasir Khusraw
items.description: After the Samanids, today's Tajikistan was divided: the Karakhanids took the north (Khujand passed between their eastern and western khanates), while Khuttal, between the Vakhsh and the Panj, kept its own autonomous rulers in the 11th–12th centuries under the loose control first of the Ghaznavids and from the mid-11th century of the Seljuks; it then passed to the Ghurids and the Khwarazmshahs. The poet, philosopher and Isma'ili missionary Nasir Khusraw was born in Qubodiyon in 1004 and died in Yamgan in Badakhshan; the Isma'ilis of Badakhshan, today's Pamiris, revere him as their founder. In 2025 eleven sites of medieval Khuttal, including Buddhist temples, palaces and caravanserais, were inscribed as a World Heritage Site.

items.name: Mongols, the Qara'unas amirs and Timur
items.description: The Mongols conquered the Khwarezmian Empire in 1219–1221, sacking Bukhara and Samarkand, and the land became part of Chagatai's ulus. In 1346 Qazaghan, amir of the Qara'unas, killed the Chagatai khan Qazan; for twelve years he ruled the western ulus through puppet khans, until he was assassinated in 1358. His grandson Amir Husayn and the young Timur then fought together against the Moghul khans: after Tughlugh Timur's death (1363) they took Transoxiana and in 1365 drove out his son Ilyas Khoja. They then fell out, and in 1370 Timur besieged Husayn in Balkh and had him executed, becoming master of Transoxiana. Khuttal re-emerged as an autonomous principality in this period. The Sufi Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani, who died in 1384, is buried in Kulob, where his shrine still stands. The Timurids held Hisar and Khuttal until the Uzbeks came.

items.name: Bukhara's beks, Hisar, Karategin and the Pamir statelets
items.description: Muhammad Shaybani's Uzbeks took Hisar in 1504; Babur briefly won it back in 1511. Hisar became a semi-independent principality that furnished troops to Bukhara, Kulob (then called Khatlon) joined the Khanate of Bukhara in 1559, and Hisar was usually subordinate to the khan's relative in Balkh. Dushanbe first appears in the records in 1676 as a market town under Balkh, named after its Monday (dushanbe) bazaar. After 1711 Bukhara's decline let Hisar assert its independence, which lasted until 1868; Karategin, the Rasht valley, was ruled by native princes who claimed descent from Alexander, and the mountain statelets of Darvaz, Shughnan-Rushan and Wakhan ruled the Western Pamirs. The Khanate of Kokand took Ura-Tyube and Khujand in the early 19th century.

items.name: Russian Turkestan, the Emirate of Bukhara and the Pamirs
items.description: In 1866 Khujand became part of Russian Turkestan. Defeated by Russia in 1868, the Emirate of Bukhara became a Russian protectorate in 1873; with Russian help it brought Hisar and the Dushanbe region back under its rule and in 1877 conquered Karategin and Darvaz. 'Eastern Bukhara', today's central and southern Tajikistan, was governed by the emir's beks. In the Pamirs, Russian expeditions mapped the mountains from 1871; Britain and Russia agreed an Afghan frontier along the Panj in 1873, Russian troops built a fort near Murghab in 1893 and moved their base to Khorog in 1895–96, and the 1895–96 settlement created the Wakhan Corridor between the Russian and British empires. In July 1916 protests against wartime labour conscription turned violent in Khujand. In September 1920 the Red Army overthrew the last emir, Alim Khan.

items.name: Soviet Tajikistan: from ASSR to Union republic
items.description: The Basmachi revolt against Soviet rule was strongest in eastern Bukhara, where the Lakai leader Ibrahim Bek fought the Red Army; he later raided from Afghanistan until Tajik villagers captured him, and he was executed on 31 August 1931. On 14 October 1924 the Tajik ASSR was created inside the Uzbek SSR from eastern Bukhara, with its capital at Dyushambe, a village of 3,000 people in 1920, and in 1925 the Pamirs became the autonomous Gorno-Badakhshan. On 5 December 1929 Tajikistan became a full Union republic, gaining the north (today's Sughd) with Khujand, while Bukhara and Samarkand stayed in Uzbekistan; Dyushambe was renamed Stalinabad and became Dushanbe again in 1961. The Nurek Dam on the Vakhsh, built from 1961 to 1980, was then the tallest dam in the world.

items.name: Independence and the civil war
items.description: Tajikistan declared independence on 9 September 1991. In May 1992 fighting broke out between the government of Rahmon Nabiyev, backed by groups from Khujand and Kulob, and an opposition of democrats and Islamists drawn largely from Garm and Gorno-Badakhshan, which briefly declared its own independence. The civil war killed an estimated 20,000 to 150,000 people and displaced 10–20% of the population. Emomali Rahmon came to power in 1994, and on 27 June 1997 he and the United Tajik Opposition leader Sayid Abdulloh Nuri signed the peace agreement in Moscow. Rahmon has ruled since; Russian troops guarded the Afghan border until 2005, and in 2020 he was re-elected for another seven years.
